title: How Far Ahead to Look: The Lookahead Is a Gain

questions.question: Steering by a perfect pose, is there any reason to use a long lookahead?
options: No: shorter tracks better at every value measured, and the corner cut grows in proportion to it
Yes, a long lookahead is smoother and equally accurate
Yes, a short lookahead always oscillates
It makes no difference either way
questions.explanation: Measured on a right angle: 0.0176 m worst error at 0.10 m of lookahead, 1.3536 m at 5.00 m. The reason to lengthen it is that no follower ever steers by a perfect pose.

questions.question: The pose estimate is 100 ms behind and the robot drives at 1 m/s. Lookaheads of 0.05, 0.10, 0.20 and 0.40 m are tried. Which work?
options: 0.20 and 0.40: everything at or below speed times latency loses the path entirely
All of them, with the shorter ones tracking better
Only 0.40, since latency needs a large margin
All of them fail, since the estimate is late
questions.explanation: The threshold moved exactly with speed: at 0.5 m/s the first working lookahead was 0.10, at 2 m/s it was 0.40, and at 4 m/s none of the four worked.

questions.question: With 2 cm of pose noise and no latency, a lookahead of 0.10 m tracked slightly better than 0.80 m. Where did the noise show up?
options: In the steering: the churn was 3.58 against 0.075, about fifty times as much movement for the same corner
In the tracking error, which was much worse
Nowhere, since the follower averages it out
In the corner cut, which grew
questions.explanation: Noise is paid for in the actuator and latency in the path. Telling them apart matters because they have different fixes and only one of them loses the robot.

questions.question: The planner clears an obstacle by 20 cm and the robot clips it, while reporting 3 cm rms tracking error. What happened?
options: The lookahead cut the corner by about 27 percent of itself, and cross track error is not a clearance figure
The follower's tracking error report is wrong
The estimate was late, so the robot was not where it thought
The path was too finely sampled
questions.explanation: Measured, the corner cut was 0.266 to 0.271 of the lookahead across two decades of it. If the requirement is about obstacles, the acceptance test has to measure distance to obstacles.

questions.question: Why must the target search never look back before the last target it found?
options: On a path that returns near itself, an earlier point is also more than a lookahead away and comes first in the array
It would be too slow to search the whole path
The path may be modified while driving
Points behind the robot have negative curvature
questions.explanation: Measured on a 20 m path with two parallel legs 0.6 m apart: searching from the start, the robot never turned once and drove 80 m in a straight line before the test gave up.

questions.question: What does an acceptance path for a follower need that a straight line does not have?
options: A corner, a section that comes back near itself, and a speed change
Enough length to reach steady state
Waypoints spaced closely enough to be smooth
A start and end at the same point
questions.explanation: Each of those exposes a different failure in this lesson: the corner shows the cut, the returning leg shows the target search, and the speed change shows a fixed lookahead that is only correct at the speed it was tuned at.
